item.source_question_text:
Which of the following statements is correct?
A. We can assume a "spherical cow" when analyzing the motion of a cow's leg. [incorrect]
B. We can safely assume a cow is a point mass when analyzing its position change in the scale of a mile over a certain time period. [correct]
C. We can never assume the cow is in a vacuum, even when we need to ignore the effect of air resistance. [incorrect]
D. None of the above is correct. [incorrect]
item.generated_question_text:
Which of the following statements about using simplified physical models is correct?
A. We can model a gymnast’s hand as a point mass when analyzing the torque in a wrist rotation. This is incorrect because torque about the wrist depends on how mass is distributed, so a point-mass hand model typically throws away the needed geometry. [incorrect]
B. We can model a delivery truck as a point mass when estimating how far it travels on a highway over tens of kilometers. This is correct because over long travel distances the truck’s size is negligible compared with the displacement, so a point-mass model captures position change well. [correct]
C. We should never assume motion occurs in a vacuum, even when we are explicitly neglecting air drag. This is incorrect because “neglect air resistance” is effectively the same modeling move as treating the situation like a vacuum for that effect. [incorrect]
D. None of the above is correct. This is incorrect because option B is a valid approximation for long-range translational motion. [incorrect]

A. It stays the same. [incorrect]
B. It decreases by a factor of 31/2. [incorrect]
C. It increases by a factor of 3. [correct]
D. It increases by a factor of 9. [incorrect]
E. It increases by a factor of 31/2. [incorrect]
item.generated_question_text:
If the magnitudes of both charges are doubled and their separation is quadrupled, what happens to the magnitude of the electrostatic force that each charge exerts on the other?
A. It stays the same. This is incorrect because F ∝ q1q2/r2 changes when q and r scale differently. [incorrect]
B. It decreases by a factor of 4. This is correct because doubling both charges gives a factor of 4 while quadrupling separation gives a factor of 16 in the denominator, so F scales by 4/16 = 1/4. [correct]
C. It increases by a factor of 2. This is incorrect because it undercounts the squared dependence on separation and the product of the two charges. [incorrect]
D. It increases by a factor of 4. This is incorrect because it accounts for the charge scaling but ignores that r2 grows by 16. [incorrect]
E. It decreases by a factor of 16. This is incorrect because it considers only the separation change and forgets that the charges also increase the force by a factor of 4. [incorrect]

item.source_question_text:
A 4.5 kg cart initially moving at 2.1 m/s collides with a wall and rebounds at a speed of 1.3 m/s moving backward. The collision lasts for a 0.2 seconds. What is the average force exerted on the cart during the collision?
A. 47.3 N. [incorrect]
B. 18 N. [incorrect]
C. 76.5 N. [correct]
D. None of the above is correct. [incorrect]
item.generated_question_text:
A 2.8 kg cart initially moving at 3.0 m/s collides with a wall and rebounds at a speed of 1.0 m/s moving backward. The collision lasts for 0.25 seconds. What is the average force exerted on the cart during the collision?
A. 44.8 N. This is correct because Δp = m(vf − vi) = 2.8(−1.0 − 3.0) = −11.2 N · s, so |Favg| = |Δp|/Δt = 11.2/0.25 = 44.8 N. [correct]
B. 11.2 N. This is incorrect because it confuses the impulse magnitude |Δp| (in N·s) with force (in N) by forgetting to divide by time. [incorrect]
C. 22.4 N. This is incorrect because it effectively uses only part of the velocity change (e.g., subtracting speeds instead of accounting for reversal of direction). [incorrect]
D. None of the above is correct. This is incorrect because option A correctly computes the average force magnitude. [incorrect]
